tagline: A letter from prison about God's plan to gather all things in Christ, and about the one new people, Jew and Gentile together, that his grace has made.
overview:
Ephesians is a letter in two halves. The first three chapters are praise, prayer, and teaching: God chose a people in Christ before the world began, raised them from spiritual death by grace alone, and in the cross tore down the wall that divided Jews from Gentiles, so that the two now make one body, one household, one temple where God lives by his Spirit. The last three chapters turn that teaching into life: walk worthy of this calling, keep the unity the Spirit has made, put off the old self and put on the new, live out the gospel in marriage, family, and work, and stand firm against the spiritual powers of evil in the armor God supplies.

The letter has little of the controversy that drives Galatians or Corinthians. There is no false teacher to answer and no named crisis. Instead it steps back and looks at the whole of what God is doing, a plan that reaches from before the foundation of the world to the fullness of time, when he will bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ (1:10). The church is at the center of that picture, not as an institution but as the first sign of a reconciled creation.

Few books have shaped Christian thinking about grace and the church as much as this one. Its summary of salvation, “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (2:8-9), became a touchstone of the Reformation. Its household instructions (5:21-6:9) remain some of the most debated verses in the New Testament, both for what they say about marriage and for how they were later used to defend slavery.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author twice (1:1 and 3:1), and the early church received it as his without question. It is well attested among second-century Christian writers, and until the modern period almost no one doubted it.

Since the nineteenth century many scholars have argued that it was written after Paul's death by a follower writing in his name, a practice (called pseudonymity) that some think was an accepted way to carry a teacher's thought forward. Their reasons are these: the Greek style is unlike the letters nearly everyone accepts as Paul's, with very long sentences (1:3-14 is a single sentence in Greek); the vocabulary and emphases differ, with salvation spoken of as already completed (2:5-8) and the church as universal rather than local; the apostles and prophets are described as the church's foundation (2:20), which reads to some like a later generation looking back; the letter closely parallels Colossians, as if one were built from the other; and it sounds impersonal for a man who spent more than two years in Ephesus (1:15 and 3:2 speak as if Paul and the readers knew each other only by report).

Many other scholars defend Paul's authorship. Style varies with subject, and a letter of praise and prayer will read differently from a letter of argument. Paul commonly used a secretary, which could account for differences in wording. The overlap with Colossians fits one writer composing two letters at about the same time and sending both with Tychicus (6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-8). The impersonal tone is explained if the letter was meant for several churches, not Ephesus alone. And the early church, which did reject some writings as falsely attributed, accepted this one. Both positions are held by careful, faithful scholars; readers on both sides agree the letter carries Paul's gospel.
date: If Paul wrote it, he did so as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20), most likely during his house arrest in Rome, traditionally dated around AD 60 to 62, at about the same time as Colossians and Philemon. Some who accept Paul's authorship place it during an earlier imprisonment, in Caesarea around AD 57 to 59 or possibly in Ephesus in the mid-50s. Scholars who think a later follower wrote it usually date it between about AD 80 and 100. It must be earlier than the early second century, when Christian writers already appear to know it.
setting:
Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire, a port on the western coast of what is now Turkey and the leading city of the Roman province of Asia. It was famous for its temple of Artemis, counted among the wonders of the ancient world, and for its trade in magic and religious objects. Acts 19 tells how Paul spent more than two years there, teaching daily in a lecture hall, how books of magic worth a great sum were burned by new believers, and how a riot broke out when silversmiths who made shrines of Artemis saw their trade threatened. From Ephesus the gospel spread through the surrounding province.

There is a textual question in the letter's first verse. The words “in Ephesus” (1:1) are missing from the earliest surviving manuscripts, including a papyrus from about AD 200 and the two great fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus in their original form. The second-century teacher Marcion knew the letter under the title To the Laodiceans. For these reasons many scholars think the letter was a circular, meant to be carried from church to church in the province of Asia, with Ephesus as its best-known destination; some connect it with the letter from Laodicea mentioned in Colossians 4:16. Others think the words are original and were dropped in some copies. Either way, the readers were mostly Gentile believers (2:11; 3:1) in the cities of western Asia Minor, living among temples, guilds, and household religion, and needing to understand who they now were.
purpose: Ephesians is written to Gentile Christians to tell them who they are in Christ and how to live as that people. It aims to deepen their grasp of God's grace and power (1:15-23; 3:14-21), to show them that they have been joined to Israel's hope and to Jewish believers as one body (2:11-3:13), and to teach them to live out that unity in ordinary life: in speech, sexuality, work, marriage, parenting, and the household. Its closing call to stand in God's armor (6:10-20) reminds readers living in a city full of spiritual rivals that the church's struggle is not finally with people but with the powers of evil, and that Christ has already been seated far above them (1:20-21).
story: Ephesians looks back to the promises God made to Abraham and to Israel, the covenants of the promise from which Gentiles were once strangers (2:12), and announces that in Christ those promises now include the nations. It stands after the events of Acts, reflecting a church that has become mostly Gentile and that must learn to be one people with Jewish believers. Among Paul's letters it belongs with Colossians, Philemon, and Philippians as the Prison Letters. Its vision reaches forward to the end of the story, when all things in heaven and on earth are brought together in Christ (1:10), the same horizon Revelation paints as a new heaven and a new earth.
christ: Christ is the center of everything in Ephesians. The phrase “in Christ” and its equivalents run through the letter: every blessing, the choosing, the redemption, the forgiveness, and the sealing with the Spirit happen “in Him” (1:3-14). God raised Christ from the dead and seated him above every power in the heavenly realms, and made him head over all things for the church, which is his body (1:20-23). By his blood and in his flesh he made peace between Jew and Gentile and between both and God (2:13-18). He ascended and gave gifts to his people (4:7-11), and his self-giving love for the church is the pattern for marriage (5:25). The letter also shows the Father, Son, and Spirit working together in salvation, which later Christians recognized as a witness to the Trinity.
reading: Read Ephesians slowly and read it whole. The long sentences of the opening chapters are prayer and praise, not tangled argument, and they are best read aloud. Watch for the hinge at 4:1, where teaching turns to instruction with the word “then”: the letter's commands grow out of what God has already done, and cutting them off from chapters 1 to 3 turns grace into moralism. Watch the key words: grace, in Christ, mystery, body, walk, and the heavenly realms. The household instructions (5:21-6:9) should be read against the Roman household of the first century, whose structure Paul did not invent, and with attention to how he reshapes it, opening with a call to submit to one another (5:21, read by some as mutual submission among all believers and by others as submission within ordered relationships) and holding the powerful to account before Christ. A common misreading treats the letter's language of choosing and predestination as abstract speculation; in context it is praise, meant to give believers confidence and humility.

structure.title: Greeting and blessing
structure.summary: Paul greets the saints and praises the Father for every spiritual blessing in Christ: chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, and sealed with the Spirit.

structure.title: A prayer for understanding
structure.summary: Paul prays that readers will know their hope, their inheritance, and the power that raised Christ and seated him over every rule and authority.

structure.title: Saved by grace, made one
structure.summary: Dead in sin, believers are made alive with Christ by grace through faith; Gentiles once far away are brought near, and Jew and Gentile become one new humanity and one temple.

structure.title: The mystery revealed and a second prayer
structure.summary: Paul explains his calling to make known the mystery that Gentiles are fellow heirs, then prays that readers will grasp the immeasurable love of Christ.

structure.title: Walking worthy of the calling
structure.summary: Keep the unity of the Spirit, use Christ's gifts to build up the body, put off the old self and put on the new, and walk in love, light, and wisdom.

structure.title: The Christian household
structure.summary: Mutual submission shapes the relationships of wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters, all under the one Lord.

structure.title: The armor of God and farewell
structure.summary: Believers stand against the spiritual forces of evil in God's armor and pray; Paul commends Tychicus and closes with peace and grace.

themes.title: Grace
themes.body: Salvation in Ephesians is God's work from first to last. God chose, God predestined, God lavished grace, God made the dead alive. Human beings contribute nothing but the need; even faith is the way the gift is received, not a work that earns it. Yet grace is not idle: believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works that God prepared in advance (2:10). Grace both saves and sets to work.

themes.title: One new humanity
themes.body: The deepest division of Paul's world, between Jew and Gentile, has been overcome in the cross. Christ has torn down the dividing wall of hostility and made the two into one new man (2:14-15). This is not a side topic but the heart of the mystery Paul was given to preach (3:6). The church is meant to be a visible display, even to the powers in the heavenly realms, that God can make one people out of enemies (3:10).

themes.title: The church as body, temple, and bride
themes.body: Ephesians gives the church three great pictures. It is the body of Christ, with Christ as its head, growing as each part does its work (4:15-16). It is a holy temple, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, where God dwells by the Spirit (2:20-22). And it is the bride whom Christ loved and gave himself up for, to make her holy (5:25-27). Each picture presents the church as more than a voluntary club.

themes.title: The powers
themes.body: Ephesians speaks more than any other of Paul's letters about rulers, authorities, and powers in the heavenly realms. Christ has been seated far above them all (1:21), the church makes God's wisdom known to them (3:10), and believers struggle not against flesh and blood but against them (6:12). The letter takes spiritual evil seriously without making it the center: the center is Christ's victory, and the believer's task is to stand.

themes.title: A worthy walk
themes.body: The verb “walk” marks the letter's practical half: walk worthy of the calling (4:1), no longer as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Christian life is described as a way of walking, a whole manner of conduct, shaped by the new identity God has given rather than by rules alone.

keyChapters.why: One of the great passages of praise in the Bible, setting out God's plan to bring all things together in Christ and the blessings believers receive in him.
The classic statement of salvation by grace through faith, followed by the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile into one new humanity through the cross.
The turn from teaching to life: the unity of the Spirit, the gifts of the ascended Christ to build up the body, and the call to put on the new self.
Contains the most debated passage on Christian marriage, which ties husband and wife to the relationship between Christ and the church.
Closes the household instructions with children, parents, slaves, and masters, and gives the well-known picture of the armor of God.
